title: Balancing Loops
hook: Every time you try to change how things run, something pushes back. That's normal, not failure.
statement: Systems resist change, and the bigger the change, the harder they push back.
explainer: Teams, habits, and customers all drift back to how things were. Pushing harder usually makes it worse. Lowering the friction around the change works better.
sop: Name the change you want and where you're getting pushback.
Score your Desired state and Current state 1 to 10.
Reduce friction around the change instead of adding pressure.
Hold the new way steady for at least 3 to 4 weeks.
Expect a plateau. That's the system pushing back, not failure.
equation_example: Desired state 9, Current state 4. Gap = 9 - 4 = 5. A bigger gap means more resistance, because you're asking the system to move further. A shrinking gap means the change is starting to stick.
question: Name one change that's getting pushback and one friction you could remove instead of pushing harder.
closing_statement: Expect resistance in proportion to how far you push.
caption:
Principle Nº 122: Balancing Loops

Every time you try to change how things run, something pushes back. That's normal, not failure.

Systems resist change, and the bigger the change, the harder they push back.

Your turn: Name one change that's getting pushback and one friction you could remove instead of pushing harder.
